ground_truth.title: 8 Steps To Become a Freelance Web Developer in 2026
ground_truth.author: The Upwork Team
ground_truth.main_content:
Being a freelance web developer can give you more flexibility and greater control over your career. You can choose whether you want to do front-end, back-end, or full-stack web development, and select the types of projects you want to specialize in. Instead of working full time for one employer, you can work directly with individual clients and enjoy the perks of being self-employed.

Freelance web development can be incredibly rewarding, but it also comes with challenges. In exchange for more freedom, you also have more responsibility.

If you're curious about becoming a freelance web developer, this is the place to start. In this step-by-step guide, you'll find information on how to get started and why so many people are choosing to work as independent professionals.

Let's review eight steps to kickstart your career as a freelance web developer.

1. Define your skills

The best place to start is a skills audit. Write down a list of all the skills you currently have and the ones you'd like to develop. Define what you know, what you don't know, and what you're best at and enjoy doing. Think about your career goals and what your dream workweek looks like.

Knowing your strengths and weaknesses can help you choose projects that will strengthen your portfolio and reputation. A successful freelance web development career is built on positioning yourself as a skilled professional and backing it up with positive client reviews and work samples. This helps to establish trust with new clients.

To help evaluate your skills and decide if freelancing as a web developer is the right career path for you, ask yourself these questions:
What programming languages do you prefer working in?
What type of projects do you have experience working on?
What aspects of web development do you struggle with the most?
Do you want to work in an office?
Could you see yourself in a client-facing role?
Do you like working independently?
Do you mind doing administrative tasks like invoicing?
Would you be comfortable pitching your services to clients?

2. Fill your skills gaps and enhance your education

You can take online web development courses and even earn certifications in specific languages or specialized areas of development. Some examples include:
Web Design for Everybody: Basics of Web Development & Coding Specialization
The Complete Full-Stack Web Development Bootcamp
IBM: Introduction to Web Development with HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript.
Codeacademy's Learn HTML

Many websites use WordPress, which can also be a good foundational platform to learn. The growth in eCommerce may make Shopify a valuable system to understand as well. Make sure you have the basics down and then look at more complex areas of specialization, such as Node.js or Ruby on Rails.

3. Find helpful tools

Think about what tools you need to be successful as a freelancer. If you work directly with your clients rather than on a platform like Upwork, you can avoid paying service fees (Upwork ranges from 0 to 15%, depending on the contract), but you'll need to handle many business tasks on your own. You may need to create templates for proposals and invoicing, and search for online tools that will make the processes easier.

If you work on a platform like Upwork, you should be able to easily manage business and administrative tasks with automation and integrated tools. You could help streamline productivity with additional project management, organization, and time-tracking tools.

Below, we cover some tools you could incorporate into your freelance business to streamline your workflow.

Project management

These tools help teams organize, track, and execute projects efficiently, ensuring streamlined collaboration and task visibility.
Trello. Visual project management with boards and cards, ideal for simple task tracking and team collaboration.
Hive. All-in-one tool with tasks, chat, and analytics, customizable for complex workflows and cross-team collaboration.
ClickUp. Flexible project management with tasks, goals, and docs; suited for teams needing extensive customization.
Asana. Task and project tracking with timelines and workload views, popular for clear team planning and task prioritization.

Time tracking

Time-tracking tools allow individuals and teams to log hours, manage budgets, and increase productivity by understanding where time is spent.
Harvest. Tracks time and expenses with invoicing capabilities; integrates smoothly with other project management tools.
Wrike. Time tracking within a project management system, ideal for teams needing integrated task and time management.
Everhour. Real-time tracking with reporting and budgeting; integrates with tools like Asana and Trello.
Toggl Track. User-friendly time tracking with reports and reminders, great for freelancers and small teams.

Mock-ups

Mock-up tools support designers in creating and sharing visual prototypes, enabling feedback and iteration throughout the design process.
Canva. Easy-to-use design tool with templates; suitable for creating quick mock-ups, presentations, and social media graphics.
Notism. Collaboration-focused mock-up tool with feedback features, designed for teams needing visual project discussions.
Adobe Portfolio. Showcases creative work with customizable layouts; useful for designers building an online portfolio.
Figma. Collaborative design and prototyping tool; ideal for teams working on real-time web or app designs.

AI

AI is changing the way work gets done. These tools provide automation and assistance for tasks ranging from content creation to coding, enhancing productivity and creativity.
ChatGPT. Language model for content draft generation, coding assistance, and idea brainstorming, flexible across industries.
Tabnine. AI code completion for multiple languages, integrates with popular IDEs to boost developer productivity.
Midjourney. AI image generation tool known for high-quality art creation based on user prompts, popular among designers.
GitHub Copilot. AI code assistant developed with GitHub; enhances coding speed by suggesting code in real time.
Uizard. Turns sketches into digital mock-ups, useful for designers and nondesigners creating app and web prototypes quickly.

4. Create your business plan

Being a freelancer means owning your own business, so you get to choose which projects you say yes to and often what hours you work. You're self-employed and responsible for everything from finding clients to paying taxes. Creating your business plan is integral to becoming a freelance web developer.

Your business plan acts as a roadmap, helping you outline what services you'll offer as a coder and how you plan to find your clients. Consider your top skills and the types of projects you want to take on. Many freelancers find success by choosing a niche and working hard to become experts in that space.

5. Build your portfolio

Once you have a solid business plan, it's time to build your portfolio. This living collection highlights your projects and past work to show customers what you can do. Portfolios are essential for any freelance business — especially web development — and help prospects know that you can do the work they need. By reviewing past projects, clients can quickly get a feel for your work quality and style. 

You can create an entire portfolio website dedicated to your work if you're freelancing off-platform or have many different types of examples, or you can add your best work to your Upwork portfolio. Think of the portfolio as your storefront, where people can browse and choose options. This means showcasing a diverse selection of high-quality work to attract more customers.

Create an online portfolio with Upwork

Your Upwork portfolio lives on your profile, with your overview, reviews, experience, testimonials, and other important information that clients want to see before making a decision. If you plan on finding clients through Upwork, having an impressive portfolio can help you win proposals and projects. Check out these web developer portfolios for inspiration.

6. Conduct market research

Market research is key to establishing yourself in freelance web development. It helps you understand client needs, industry trends, and competitor strategies so you can stand out. Here's how to conduct market research effectively:
Stay updated on trends. Follow industry blogs and forums to learn the latest in tools and design — keeping your skills relevant. You can quickly get information on salaries, hourly rates, and in-demand skills.
Analyze competitor portfolios. Review other freelancers' work to spot opportunities and see where you can offer something unique.
Engage in online communities. Join forums to hear client pain points firsthand, allowing you to target their specific needs.
Network with other programmers. Many experienced professionals are willing to network and share tips on how they got started, as well as share their initial rates. Gather as much information as you can on potential customers and competition. Knowing what people need can help you figure out your angle and competitive edge to win more proposals.
Conduct keyword research. Discover popular keywords to frame your services in the languages clients search for.
Survey potential clients. Direct feedback from potential clients informs your approach to pricing and service offerings.
Review job listings. Analyze freelance job boards to understand what skills are in demand and align your profile accordingly. Joining groups on LinkedIn and Facebook can help you understand what's in demand locally, too. Online communities like Reddit can also be valuable resources for input and problem-solving help.

With focused market research, you'll be better equipped to position yourself as a competitive freelance web developer.

7. Apply for jobs

Upwork is a great platform for building a freelance career in nearly any field, and web development is one of the top in-demand skills on the platform. On Upwork, you can browse the Talent Marketplace and filter jobs based on your skill set and criteria, like hourly rate, hours per week, experience level, and more. 

When you find a project that you like and want to apply to, make sure to read the entire post. Many companies and clients have specific requirements and needs for their jobs. The best proposals address these specific items. Demonstrate your know-how and understanding. Take your time creating each proposal and remember to proofread your submission.

8. Create your marketing strategy

Once you're ready to start accepting clients, you need to figure out how you'll market yourself. As a freelancer, you're a small business owner, so marketing your services and other admin tasks are important facets of the job.

To create a practical marketing strategy to launch your freelance web development career, you should:
Define your niche and services. Identify the specific web development services you'll offer and consider specializing in a niche, like eCommerce sites or responsive design, to differentiate yourself.
Create a strong portfolio. Showcase your skills with a portfolio that highlights past projects, client testimonials, and the impact of your work; focus on quality over quantity.
Set competitive pricing. Research market rates for freelance web programmers with similar skills and experience, and consider offering flexible pricing packages for different client needs.
Develop an online presence. Build a website or landing page that outlines your services, portfolio, and contact details; keep it optimized for search engines to attract organic traffic.
Use social media strategically. Share your work, insights, and web development tips on platforms like LinkedIn, X, and GitHub to build a professional network and engage potential clients.
Leverage freelancing platforms. Establish profiles on sites like Upwork to access a wider client base and gain experience, especially when starting out.
Gather and share testimonials. Request feedback from past clients and display these testimonials on your website and social profiles to build trust and credibility.
Use content marketing. Write blog posts, guides, or tutorials on web development topics relevant to your services, helping to position you as an expert and attract inbound leads.
Invest in targeted ads. Consider running ads on platforms like Google or LinkedIn to reach potential clients searching for web development services.
Optimize for SEO. Use keywords that clients are likely to search for, such as "freelance web developer" or "custom website design," to increase your visibility on search engines.
Build long-term client relationships. Whether you're working with established companies or fast-growing startups, prioritize clear communication, deliver quality work, and offer ongoing support to encourage repeat business and referrals.

Each of these steps helps build a foundation for finding clients, establishing credibility, and creating a sustainable freelance web development business.

Launch your web developer career today

Today can be day one of your new career. If you're not quite ready to take on clients, you can work on filling your skills gaps and learning the web development skills that clients are looking for.

Every step you take gets you closer to your goal. Once you're ready to take on freelance work, start browsing web developer jobs on Upwork. Let us help you land your first client! 

FAQ about becoming a freelance web developer

Let's review some of the most common questions about this career choice.

What are the benefits of being a freelance web developer?

Many developers transition to a freelance career because of the flexibility and freedom they can have as independent professionals. As a freelancer, you have more control over your career and can create a schedule that fits your lifestyle as long as you meet your clients' demands and expectations.

Here are some benefits of being a freelance web developer that you might enjoy most:
Diverse clients. Instead of just one employer, you have clients who may be very different from one another. With diversity, you have flexibility and generally availability of clients. You get to switch up what you do and have more variety in your workweek.
Numerous opportunities. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the expected growth rate in web development and digital design is 7%, which is much higher than the average. As freelancing becomes more mainstream, more companies than ever before are turning to independent professionals.
Control over projects. If you prefer a type of development, you can focus on that and work on becoming an expert. While you may sometimes need to accept jobs just to pay the bills, as you grow your reputation and the demand for your services rises, you can start saying yes to your preferred jobs and no to others.
Work from wherever. All you need as a web developer is your computer and a strong internet connection. This gives you the freedom to work from almost anywhere you want, whether that's from home, a local coffee shop, or even a vacation spot.
Set your own hours. As a freelance software developer, you have the flexibility to decide when you want to work. But, even though you control your hours, you'll still need to be available at certain times for meetups to connect with clients for project discussions, progress updates, or team coordination.
Grow your career on your own terms. Growing your reputation as an expert in a specialty can help increase the demand for your services so you can raise your rates. People tend to be faster and better at the work they enjoy doing, which is an added incentive.

What skills does a freelance web developer need?

Successful freelance web developers know the importance of complementing their technical expertise with relevant soft skills and hard skills. Clients want web software engineers who make the overall experience simple and stress-free.

Even if you're incredibly talented at the technical work you do, having valuable soft skills is essential for positive feedback, referrals, and repeat clients.

We discuss some of the soft and hard skills and traits of a good freelance web developer that clients look for:

Soft skills include:
Communication
Reliability
Accountability
Willingness to help or start new projects

Hard skills include:
Programming languages
Web development frameworks such as React, Django, and Ruby on Rails
Version control systems such as Git

Popular front-end development languages include:
HTML
CSS
JavaScript
React
Swift

Popular back-end development languages include:
PHP
SQL
Python
Java
Ruby
C#

Beyond knowing those languages, other hard skills that successful web developers should learn and keep updated include:
Search engine optimization (SEO)
Testing and debugging
Responsive web design (making websites work across devices)
UX and UI (creating a user-friendly experience and interface)
Web hosting
Cybersecurity
APIs (being able to integrate client software and programs)
Database management
Content management systems (CMS)

What types of freelance web developers are there?

Most freelancers focus on a specific niche and then work to position themselves as experts at what they do. Web development has two sides — the front end and the back end. As a web developer, you can specialize in one of these or do both, called full-stack. Having a niche, even if it's full-stack, helps you to focus on building your reputation, which can increase the demand for your skills so you can raise your rates and earn more clients.

Front-end

Front-end developers enjoy the design aspect of development. They focus on the part that the user interacts with: the user interface (UI). Front-end software developers think heavily about the user experience (UX) and how to make the website easy to use, accessible, and overall aesthetically pleasing. This type of web development can focus on the layout, graphics, navigation, how to display content, and even go into typography and color schemes.

If you enjoy visuals and have an eye for design and creativity, you may like front-end development best. As a front-end developer, you still need technical skills like proficiency with programming languages, but the focus is on the visual aspect of the website.

You may work with the client to create mock-ups and wireframes, determining what elements the website needs at a technical level. The client will often take this to a back-end developer, who builds the website's foundation and then hands it back to you so you can continue to work on the front end.

Back-end

Back-end web developers work behind the scenes, writing the code to build the website's framework. As a back-end developer, you're responsible for the coding stored on web servers. You create the code that makes the website run. Back-end web developers think most about databases, APIs, cybersecurity, and website performance.

If you're interested in being a programmer and building websites but want to concentrate on performance rather than visuals, back-end development may be what you'll find most appealing. While you still have to consider design and UX, you'll focus more on building the functionality and structure, and then hand it over to the front-end developer.

As a back-end developer, you'll have to work with your client to figure out what they want before you can start building. The client may have a project manager, UX designer, front-end developer, or another team member you'll collaborate with. Often your clients don't know what it takes behind the scenes to create certain features or integrations, so you have to understand what they want the website to look like first, and then make it possible on your end.

Full-stack

If you want to work on both the back and front ends, this is full-stack web development. As a full-stack web developer, you can offer entire packages to your clients. Instead of hiring two different web developers, they can work with just you. You'll need to know the programming languages for both sides, but you have greater control over the code and the build.

Full-stack developers work with their clients in the early stages, figuring out what they want down to the finest detail and then creating mock-ups for them to sign off on. Once you know what the client wants, you can start building the back end. After the back end, you'll work on the front end, collaborating with other stakeholders if needed to work on the layouts and visual display.

Full-stack web development was popular in the earlier stages of the Internet when websites had fewer integrations, technologies, and features. Today's full-stack web developers typically work on simpler websites or shipping minimal viable products (MVPs) for clients that then can be added to. They can shift from back end to front end, but complicated websites often require separate developers.

How much do web developers make?

What you can charge as a web developer depends on your experience and the complexity of the website. On average, web developers on Upwork make between $15 and $50 per hour.

When you're starting out, you may want to charge low rates and take on smaller projects you know you can complete successfully to build your reputation and gain positive client feedback. As the demand for your services rises and your skills improve, you can start charging as much as $200 per hour for large projects requiring coding from the ground up.

How do I get started as a freelance developer without prior experience?

Breaking into freelancing as a developer can feel daunting, but you don't need years of experience to begin. Start by building a small portfolio, which could include personal projects, contributions to open-source projects, or simple websites and apps you've created to showcase your skills. 

Once you have a few examples, create a professional profile on platforms like Upwork, Fiverr, or Toptal, where clients are often open to working with motivated beginners. You can also find projects through networking in online communities (Reddit, Discord, LinkedIn groups) or by reaching out to local small businesses that may need affordable tech help. The key is to start small, deliver excellent work, and gradually build credibility and client trust.

How do freelance web developers charge clients?

Part of being an independent professional is setting your freelance rate. Your rate may go up or down depending on the project and its complexity, but you should have a general idea of how much you want to make per hour. You can charge your clients hourly or by project as a freelance web developer. If you're working on Upwork, both options have payment protection.

Hourly

If you agree to an hourly contract on Upwork, you can track your time using the app. Hourly contracts make sure that you're paid for every hour that you work. If you're working on the project, you're on the clock. Hourly contracts pay out to freelancers weekly, which can give you steadier pay compared to fixed-priced projects.

Working hourly as a freelancer is different from working as a full-time employee. You don't get to charge your clients for the amount of time spent looking for work or doing administrative tasks like marketing or invoicing. This is one of the reasons freelancers typically charge more per hour than employees do, to make up for that time.

Fixed-price

An alternative to hourly work is billing clients by project. In your proposal, you can give a fixed price for the finished website or milestones, estimating how much time it will take you. When you work by project on Upwork, you wait until payment is in project funds for a milestone before starting work. Then, after the client approves the completion of the milestone (or 14 days have passed without action), the funds are pending for five days and then released to you.

Fixed-price projects can be more lucrative if you work faster compared to an hourly project. The project can also end up taking longer than expected, decreasing your hourly rate. Your ultimate earnings depend on how accurately you estimate the time a project needs. You can work whenever you want as long as you meet your deadlines and don't have to worry about logging hours. The downside of working by project is that you don't have as clear an idea of how much you'll earn hourly, and payouts can take longer.

How can I get my first client and grow my customer base?

Starting as a freelance web developer can feel challenging, but by focusing on building trust and showcasing your skills, you'll gradually grow your client base. Here's how to get started:
Leverage your network. Reach out to friends, family, and professional contacts to let them know you're freelancing; personal connections often make great first clients.
Offer a discounted or trial project. To gain experience and testimonials, consider taking on a project at a reduced rate or offer a small trial, showing clients the quality of your work.
Use freelancing platforms to gain visibility. Sites like Upwork are a great way to gain those first few clients, receive reviews, and expand your portfolio.
Write tailored proposals. Customize great proposals to address the client's specific needs, demonstrating that you've read their project description and understand their goals.
Demonstrate value in every client interaction. From your first contact to project delivery, show clients that you're reliable, easy to work with, and focused on adding value to their business.
Ask for testimonials and referrals. After completing a project, kindly request a testimonial and see if your client can recommend you to others, helping to grow your reputation.
Engage with industry communities and events. Attend relevant events, forums, or webinars to increase your visibility among potential clients.
Build a professional online presence. Create a LinkedIn profile or social media profile that highlights your skills, services, and any project examples or testimonials you have.
Use content marketing to demonstrate expertise. Write blogs or share insights about web development on social media, positioning yourself as an expert and attracting potential clients.



Upwork does not control, operate, or sponsor the tools or services discussed in this article, which are only provided as potential options. Each reader and company should take the time to adequately analyze and determine the tools or services that would best fit their specific needs and situation.

## FAQ about becoming a freelance web developer

Let's review some of the most common questions about this career choice.

### What are the benefits of being a freelance web developer?

Many developers transition to a freelance career because of the flexibility and freedom they can have as independent professionals. As a freelancer, you have more control over your career and can create a schedule that fits your lifestyle as long as you meet your clients' demands and expectations.

Here are some benefits of being a freelance web developer that you might enjoy most:
**Diverse clients.** Instead of just one employer, you have clients who may be very different from one another. With diversity, you have flexibility and generally availability of clients. You get to switch up what you do and have more variety in your workweek.
**Numerous opportunities.** According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the expected [growth rate in web development and digital design](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/computer-and-information-technology/web-developers.htm) is 7%, which is much higher than the average. As freelancing becomes more mainstream, more companies than ever before are turning to independent professionals.
**Control over projects.** If you prefer a type of development, you can focus on that and work on becoming an expert. While you may sometimes need to accept jobs just to pay the bills, as you grow your reputation and the demand for your services rises, you can start saying yes to your preferred jobs and no to others.
**Work from wherever.** All you need as a web developer is your computer and a strong internet connection. This gives you the freedom to work from almost anywhere you want, whether that's from home, a local coffee shop, or even a vacation spot.
**Set your own hours.** As a freelance software developer, you have the flexibility to decide when you want to work. But, even though you control your hours, you'll still need to be available at certain times for meetups to connect with clients for project discussions, progress updates, or team coordination.
**Grow your career on your own terms.** Growing your reputation as an expert in a specialty can help increase the demand for your services so you can raise your rates. People tend to be faster and better at the work they enjoy doing, which is an added incentive.

### What types of freelance web developers are there?

Most freelancers focus on a specific niche and then work to position themselves as experts at what they do. Web development has two sides — the front end and the back end. As a web developer, you can specialize in one of these or do both, called full-stack. Having a niche, even if it's full-stack, helps you to focus on building your reputation, which can increase the demand for your skills so you can raise your rates and earn more clients.

**Front-end**

[Front-end developers](https://www.upwork.com/resources/front-end-developer) enjoy the design aspect of development. They focus on the part that the user interacts with: the user interface (UI). Front-end software developers think heavily about the user experience (UX) and how to make the website easy to use, accessible, and overall aesthetically pleasing. This type of web development can focus on the layout, graphics, navigation, how to display content, and even go into typography and color schemes.

If you enjoy visuals and have an eye for design and creativity, you may like front-end development best. As a front-end developer, you still need technical skills like proficiency with programming languages, but the focus is on the visual aspect of the website.

You may work with the client to create mock-ups and wireframes, determining what elements the website needs at a technical level. The client will often take this to a back-end developer, who builds the website's foundation and then hands it back to you so you can continue to work on the front end.

**Back-end**

Back-end web developers work behind the scenes, writing the code to build the website's framework. As a back-end developer, you're responsible for the coding stored on web servers. You create the code that makes the website run. Back-end web developers think most about databases, APIs, cybersecurity, and website performance.

If you're interested in being a programmer and building websites but want to concentrate on performance rather than visuals, back-end development may be what you'll find most appealing. While you still have to consider design and UX, you'll focus more on building the functionality and structure, and then hand it over to the front-end developer.

As a back-end developer, you'll have to work with your client to figure out what they want before you can start building. The client may have a project manager, UX designer, front-end developer, or another team member you'll collaborate with. Often your clients don't know what it takes behind the scenes to create certain features or integrations, so you have to understand what they want the website to look like first, and then make it possible on your end.

**Full-stack**

If you want to work on both the back and front ends, this is full-stack web development. As a [full-stack web developer](https://www.upwork.com/resources/full-stack-developer), you can offer entire packages to your clients. Instead of hiring two different web developers, they can work with just you. You'll need to know the programming languages for both sides, but you have greater control over the code and the build.

Full-stack developers work with their clients in the early stages, figuring out what they want down to the finest detail and then creating mock-ups for them to sign off on. Once you know what the client wants, you can start building the back end. After the back end, you'll work on the front end, collaborating with other stakeholders if needed to work on the layouts and visual display.

Full-stack web development was popular in the earlier stages of the Internet when websites had fewer integrations, technologies, and features. Today's full-stack web developers typically work on simpler websites or shipping minimal viable products (MVPs) for clients that then can be added to. They can shift from back end to front end, but complicated websites often require separate developers.

### How much do web developers make?

What you can charge as a web developer depends on your experience and the complexity of the website. On average, [web developers on Upwork](https://www.upwork.com/hire/web-developers/cost/) make between $15 and $50 per hour.

When you're starting out, you may want to charge low rates and take on smaller projects you know you can complete successfully to build your reputation and gain positive client feedback. As the demand for your services rises and your skills improve, you can start charging as much as $200 per hour for large projects requiring coding from the ground up.

### How do I get started as a freelance developer without prior experience?

Breaking into freelancing as a developer can feel daunting, but you don't need years of experience to begin. Start by building a small portfolio, which could include personal projects, contributions to open-source projects, or simple websites and apps you've created to showcase your skills. 

Once you have a few examples, create a professional profile on platforms like Upwork, Fiverr, or Toptal, where clients are often open to working with motivated beginners. ### How do freelance web developers charge clients?

Part of being an independent professional is [setting your freelance rate](https://www.upwork.com/resources/how-to-set-your-freelance-rate). Your rate may go up or down depending on the project and its complexity, but you should have a general idea of how much you want to make per hour. You can charge your clients hourly or by project as a freelance web developer. If you're working on Upwork, both options have [payment protection](https://support.upwork.com/hc/en-us/articles/211062568-Upwork-Payment-Protection).

**Hourly**

If you agree to an [hourly contract](https://support.upwork.com/hc/en-us/articles/211063668-Get-Paid-for-Hourly-Contracts) on Upwork, you can [track your time using the app](https://support.upwork.com/hc/en-us/articles/211064098-Log-Time-with-Time-Tracker). Hourly contracts make sure that you're paid for every hour that you work. If you're working on the project, you're on the clock. Hourly contracts pay out to freelancers weekly, which can give you steadier pay compared to fixed-priced projects.

Working hourly as a freelancer is different from working as a full-time employee. You don't get to charge your clients for the amount of time spent looking for work or doing administrative tasks like marketing or invoicing. This is one of the reasons freelancers typically charge more per hour than employees do, to make up for that time.

**Fixed-price**

An alternative to hourly work is billing clients [by project](https://support.upwork.com/hc/en-us/articles/211063718-Get-Paid-for-Fixed-Price-Contracts). In your proposal, you can give a fixed price for the finished website or milestones, estimating how much time it will take you. When you work by project on Upwork, you wait until payment is in project funds for a milestone before starting work. Then, after the client approves the completion of the milestone (or 14 days have passed without action), the funds are pending for five days and then released to you.

Fixed-price projects can be more lucrative if you work faster compared to an hourly project. The project can also end up taking longer than expected, decreasing your hourly rate. Your ultimate earnings depend on how accurately you estimate the time a project needs. You can work whenever you want as long as you meet your deadlines and don't have to worry about logging hours. The downside of working by project is that you don't have as clear an idea of how much you'll earn hourly, and payouts can take longer.

**Demonstrate value in every client interaction.** From your first contact to project delivery, show clients that you're reliable, easy to work with, and focused on adding value to their business.
**Ask for testimonials and referrals.** After completing a project, kindly request a testimonial and see if your client can recommend you to others, helping to grow your reputation.
**Engage with industry communities and events.** Attend relevant events, forums, or webinars to increase your visibility among potential clients.
**Build a professional online presence.** Create a LinkedIn profile or social media profile that highlights your skills, services, and any project examples or testimonials you have.
**Use content marketing to demonstrate expertise.** Write blogs or share insights about web development on social media, positioning yourself as an expert and attracting potential clients.
